content: 1. Technical assistance is essential for the effective implementation of breastfeeding initiatives, ensuring that healthcare providers and facilities have the necessary tools, training, and resources to support breastfeeding practices. 2. Monitoring the implementation of breastfeeding programs is critical to assess adherence to evidence-based guidelines and to identify areas for improvement in maternity and newborn care services. 3. Continuous communication and advocacy are vital to promote the importance of breastfeeding, engage stakeholders, and ensure that breastfeeding remains a public health priority. 4. Identifying and allocating sufficient resources is necessary to sustain breastfeeding programs, including funding, personnel, and infrastructure to support mothers and newborns. 5. The Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI), developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF, focuses on protecting, promoting, and supporting breastfeeding in facilities providing maternity and newborn services. It emphasizes the implementation of evidence-based practices to improve breastfeeding rates and maternal and child health outcomes. 6. The BFHI recognizes that additional interventions are required to support breastfeeding, including antenatal care, postpartum care, community-based support, workplace accommodations, adequate maternity protection, and legislation aligned with the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes. 7. Integrating the BFHI with broader breastfeeding protection, promotion, and support efforts is critical to achieving optimal breastfeeding outcomes. 8. Reinvigorating the BFHI and ensuring adherence to evidence-based maternity and newborn care recommendations can significantly increase breastfeeding rates and improve the health of mothers and children. 9. The BFHI guidance document provides updated recommendations for implementing the initiative in maternity and newborn care facilities, as well as guidance for national or subnational coordination and management of the program. 10. The primary goal of the BFHI is to ensure that mothers and newborns receive timely and appropriate care during their stay in maternity and newborn care facilities, enabling the establishment of optimal feeding practices that promote health and development. 11. Breastfeeding is the biological norm for all mammals, including humans, and is critical for achieving global goals related to nutrition, health, survival, economic growth, and environmental sustainability. 12. WHO and UNICEF recommend initiating breastfeeding within the first hour after birth, continuing exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life, and maintaining breastfeeding with safe complementary foods up to two years or beyond. 13. Globally, only a minority of infants meet these recommendations, with 44% initiating breastfeeding within the first hour after birth, 40% exclusively breastfed for the first six months, and 45% still breastfeeding at two years of age. 14. Immediate and uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding initiation within the first hour after birth are crucial for establishing breastfeeding and improving neonatal and child survival and development. 15. Delayed initiation of breastfeeding significantly increases the risk of neonatal mortality, with a 33% higher risk for newborns who start breastfeeding 2–23 hours after birth and more than double the risk for those who start one day or later. 16. Exclusive breastfeeding for six months provides the nutrients, energy, and nurturing required for physical and neurological growth and development. Beyond six months, breastfeeding continues to provide essential nutrients and energy, preventing undernutrition, obesity, and hunger when combined with safe complementary feeding. 17. Inadequate breastfeeding practices impair the health, development, and survival of infants, children, and mothers. Improving these practices could save over 820,000 lives annually. 18. Suboptimal breastfeeding practices contribute to nearly half of diarrhea episodes and one-third of respiratory infections in children. Longer breastfeeding is associated with a 13% reduction in the likelihood of obesity and a 35% reduction in the incidence of type 2 diabetes. 19. Increasing breastfeeding rates could add $300 billion annually to the global economy by fostering smarter, more productive workers and leaders. In Brazil, adults breastfed for at least 12 months earned 33% higher incomes than those breastfed for shorter durations. 20. Breastfeeding is a sustainable, natural source of nutrition that does not pollute or require resource-intensive production. In contrast, breast-milk substitutes contribute to greenhouse gas emissions and waste generation at every stage of production, transport, preparation, and use. 21. In humanitarian settings, breastfeeding's life-saving potential is even more critical. International guidance emphasizes the need to protect, promote, and support breastfeeding in these situations to maintain or improve breastfeeding practices. 22. The BFHI is a vital component of realizing every child's right to the highest attainable standard of health while respecting every mother's right to make an informed decision about infant feeding, free from commercial interests and with the necessary support to carry out her decision. 23. Improving breastfeeding practices is a key driver for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals, including ending poverty, achieving food security, promoting health and well-being, ensuring quality education, achieving gender equality, promoting economic growth, reducing inequality, and ensuring sustainable consumption and production patterns. 24. The first hours and days of a newborn's life are critical for establishing lactation and providing mothers with the support they need to breastfeed successfully. However, this support is not always provided, as evidenced by the gap between skilled birth attendance and timely breastfeeding initiation. 25. Health professionals may inadvertently interfere with breastfeeding initiation through practices such as mother-infant separation, delayed breastfeeding initiation, pre-lacteal feeds, and unnecessary supplementation, increasing the risk of breastfeeding challenges and early cessation. 26. The Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding, published by WHO and UNICEF in 1989, outline policies and procedures that facilities providing maternity and newborn services should implement to support breastfeeding. 27. The Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative, launched in 1991, motivates facilities to implement the Ten Steps and comply with the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes to achieve Baby-Friendly designation. 28. Evidence demonstrates that adherence to the Ten Steps significantly impacts breastfeeding rates, including early initiation, exclusive breastfeeding, and total breastfeeding duration. A dose-response relationship exists between the number of steps implemented and improved breastfeeding outcomes. 29. Avoiding supplementation of newborns with products other than breast milk is a critical step in supporting successful breastfeeding.
